scenes.tts: In male C B A C a J mice, after loud noise, hearing thresholds can come back to normal. Yet the cochlea has lost about half of its ribbon synapses at one place. How can the test miss that? A threshold is only the quietest sound that gets a response. It says little about how many synapses carry the rest.

scenes.tts: Start with the inner hair cell. It releases transmitter continuously onto auditory nerve fibres, at ribbon synapses. The ribbon is a dense structure at the release site. In mouse, it keeps a larger pool of vesicles in supply. A threshold does not count these synapses.
scenes.visual: Large inner hair cell with one ribbon, a vesicle pool and a nerve terminal; vesicles drop onto the terminal; a threshold chip is set against a synapse-count chip with a not-equal sign.
scenes.narration: Start with the inner hair cell. It releases transmitter continuously onto auditory nerve fibres, at ribbon synapses. The ribbon is a dense structure at the release site. In mouse, it keeps a larger pool of vesicles in supply. A threshold does not count these synapses.

scenes.tts: Kujawa and Liberman tested this in male C B A C a J mice. They played noise at eight to sixteen kilohertz, at one hundred decibels S P L, for two hours. By two weeks, thresholds were back to their old values, and the hair cells were intact. But at eight weeks, the ribbon count at the thirty-two kilohertz place was about fifty percent below control. The nerve degenerated later.

The nerve degenerated later.
scenes.visual: Timeline: before noise, two weeks, eight weeks. Threshold marker returns to the same height; ribbon-count bar drops to about half at eight weeks.

scenes.tts: In people, no living synapse count exists. So two studies used proxies. In thirty-four young adults, the higher-risk group had a higher S P to A P ratio. The authors called it consistent with selective neural loss. But that group also had raised thresholds at ten to sixteen kilohertz. A second study compared sixteen listeners with trouble hearing speech in noise against sixteen matched controls. It found no association. The authors allowed that the measures might not be sensitive enough.
scenes.caption: In people, no living synapse count exists. So two studies used proxies. In 34 young adults, the higher-risk group had a higher SP/AP ratio. The authors called it consistent with selective neural loss. But that group also had raised thresholds at 10 to 16 kHz. A second study compared 16 listeners with trouble hearing speech in noise against 16 matched controls. It found no association. The authors allowed that the measures might not be sensitive enough.

scenes.tts: The same care applies to treatment numbers. In one child in an early O T O F gene therapy trial, the baseline A B R threshold was above the ninety-five decibel test ceiling in each ear. At week twenty-six it was fifty-eight decibels. So the improvement was more than thirty-seven decibels. That is a lower bound, not an exact value. And it is not a percentage of hearing restored.
scenes.caption: The same care applies to treatment numbers. In one child in an early OTOF gene therapy trial, the baseline ABR threshold was above the 95 dB test ceiling in each ear. At week 26 it was 58 dB. So the improvement was more than 37 dB. That is a lower bound, not an exact value. And it is not a percentage of hearing restored.

scenes.tts: A complaint, a proposed lesion and a validated test are three different things. A normal threshold did not mean intact synapses in these mice. A proxy is not a synapse count. A value past the ceiling gives a bound, not an exact change. So ask what a number counts, and what it leaves out.
